\begin{proof}
Suppose that $X=\prod_\beta X_\beta$ is Hausdorff, and fix an index $\alpha$. Since every $X_\beta$ is nonempty, choose points $a_\beta\in X_\beta$ for all $\beta\neq\alpha$. Define
\[
S=\{z\in X: z_\beta=a_\beta\text{ for every }\beta\neq\alpha\}.
\]
Then $S$ is a subspace of the Hausdorff space $X$, so $S$ is Hausdorff. The map $f:X_\alpha\to S$ given by
\[
f(x)_\alpha=x,\qquad f(x)_\beta=a_\beta\quad(\beta\neq\alpha)
\]
is a homeomorphism, with inverse the restriction of the projection $\pi_\alpha$ to $S$. Therefore $X_\alpha$ is Hausdorff.\end{proof}

\[
S=\bigcap_{\beta\neq\alpha}\pi_\beta^{-1}(\{a_\beta\})

\]
Whether or not $S$ is open or closed is irrelevant: every subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff. Define $s:X_\alpha\to S$ by inserting the chosen points in all coordinates other than $\alpha$. Then $s$ is a bijection, and $\pi_\alpha|_S$ is its continuous inverse. Hence $X_\alpha$ is homeomorphic to $S$, so $X_\alpha$ is Hausdorff.\end{proof}

\]
Let $S=s(X_\alpha)$. Since $S$ is a subspace of the Hausdorff space $X$, it is Hausdorff. The section $s:X_\alpha\to S$ is continuous, and the restriction $\pi_\alpha|_S:S\to X_\alpha$ is continuous. They are inverse maps. Therefore $X_\alpha$ is homeomorphic to the Hausdorff space $S$, and consequently $X_\alpha$ is Hausdorff.\end{proof}
